title: Where to Eat Mandu (Korean Dumplings) in Seoul: 4 Local Favorites
html:
If there is one food that's perfect for your very first meal in Korea, it's mandu — Korean dumplings. They're cheap (most bowls cost around ₩8,000–13,000, roughly $6–10 USD), filling, never spicy, and easy to order even if you don't speak a word of Korean — you can usually just point at a photo on the wall or the English menu. That makes mandu a great "safe" dish to try while you're still getting used to Korean food.

Here are four small, long-running mandu restaurants that made the MICHELIN Guide Seoul Bib Gourmand list — an award for places with great food at a reasonable price, not fancy fine dining. They're spread across four different neighborhoods, so pick whichever one is closest to the sightseeing you already have planned.

1. Gaeseong Mandu Koong — Insadong

This is one of the oldest mandu restaurants on this list — it's been open for more than 30 years. The founder was a refugee who fled to South Korea from the city of Gaeseong (now in North Korea) during the Korean War, and she brought her hometown's dumpling recipe with her. Her granddaughters now help run the restaurant. "Gaeseong-style" mandu is stuffed with pork and vegetables like cabbage and pumpkin, and the flavor is lighter and more delicate than the mandu you might find at a convenience store back home.

The restaurant's specialty is mandu jeongol, a bubbling hot pot filled with dumplings, rice cakes, mushrooms, and meat — great for sharing between two or three people. If you'd rather eat alone, order mandu-guk, a simple dumpling soup. A beginner-friendly tip: this spot is so popular with locals that it sometimes sells out of mandu before dinner time, so try to go for an early lunch.

  • Address: 11-3 Insadong 10-gil, Jongno-gu, Seoul
  • Hours: 11:30–21:30 most days (last order 20:50), Sundays 11:30–20:00 (last order 19:20), with a break from 15:00–16:00. Hours can change, so it's worth a quick call or a check on a map app before you go.
  • Good to combine with: Insadong is Seoul's best-known street for traditional crafts, tea houses, and souvenirs, so this is an easy lunch stop while you're exploring there.

2. Jaha Son Mandu — Buam-dong

Buam-dong is a quiet, hilly neighborhood tucked behind the old Seoul city wall, near the start of a popular hiking trail along the Bukhansan fortress wall. After a walk, stop here for the restaurant's signature dish: mandutguk, dumplings served in a warm beef broth. It's simple, comforting food, similar to how you might enjoy a bowl of good soup after a cold hike anywhere in the world.

One thing to plan around: this restaurant is closed on Mondays. The rest of the week it's generally open from around 11:00 to 21:00, but exact hours can shift, so check a map app on the day you plan to visit.

  • Address: 12 Baekseokdong-gil, Jongno-gu, Seoul
  • Closed: Mondays
  • Good to combine with: Hiking the Seoul city wall trail near Changuimun Gate, or a quiet walk through Buam-dong's cafes and small galleries.

3. Mandujip — Apgujeong (Gangnam)

If your trip includes shopping or people-watching in Gangnam, Mandujip is a good, down-to-earth lunch break from the area's upscale boutiques. Its dumpling soup usually comes with about six large dumplings per bowl — plenty for one person — and the restaurant also serves bindaetteok (savory mung bean pancakes) and spicy pancakes, which are good to share at the table.

A local habit worth copying: Koreans often treat a bowl of mandu-guk as a quick, no-fuss weekday lunch rather than a special occasion — it's completely normal to eat here solo and be in and out within 30 minutes.

  • Address: 338 Apgujeong-ro, Gangnam-gu, Seoul
  • Hours: Roughly midday to early evening on weekdays, with reports of an afternoon break and Sunday closures — reservations aren't usually needed, but double-check the day's hours on a map app since sources don't fully agree.
  • Good to combine with: Apgujeong Rodeo Street shopping or a walk around Cheongdam.

4. Mipildam — Hapjeong-dong (near Hongdae)

Mipildam is the smallest and most personal spot on this list. It's run by a young couple who make their mandu-guk using a recipe from the husband's grandmother, who was originally from Hwanghae Province (now part of North Korea). The broth is lightly seasoned and the dumplings are handmade, giving the whole bowl a homemade, "someone's grandma made this" kind of feel rather than a typical restaurant taste.

The restaurant is tucked into a quiet alley, so it's a nice detour if you're already near Hongdae or Hapjeong Station for the nightlife, cafes, or indie shops in that area.

  • Address: 22 Seongji 3-gil, Mapo-gu, Seoul
  • Good to know: It's a small, casual, walk-in spot — exact hours weren't easy to confirm online, so check a Korean map app (Naver Map or Kakao Map) for the current schedule before heading over.
  • Good to combine with: A day exploring Hongdae or Hapjeong's cafe streets.

Quick comparison

Restaurant Neighborhood Signature Dish Good For
Gaeseong Mandu Koong Insadong Mandu jeongol (dumpling hot pot) Groups, after sightseeing in Insadong
Jaha Son Mandu Buam-dong Mandutguk (dumpling soup in beef broth) Refueling after a city wall hike
Mandujip Apgujeong, Gangnam Dumpling soup with bindaetteok Solo travelers, quick lunch near shopping
Mipildam Hapjeong-dong Handmade mandutguk A quiet, homemade-style meal near Hongdae

💬 Tried one of these mandu spots, or have a favorite dumpling restaurant of your own in Seoul? Tell us about it in the comments below!
meta_description: A beginner's guide to 4 Michelin Bib Gourmand mandu (dumpling) restaurants across Seoul, from Insadong to Gangnam.
